activities.anchor: Milgram's variations map the pressure onto distance and dissent
activities.caption: order the variations, most to least obedience
activities.name: socVariationsOrder

config.prompt: Milgram's variations, most to least full obedience — order them:
items: A shabby downtown office — full obedience around 48%
Same-room proximity — teacher and learner within sight, around 40%
A second authority who says 'stop' — collapsed towards zero
config.why: The gradient maps pressure onto distance and dissent — agency theory reads it as people shifting into an agentic state, 'I was following orders', outsourcing moral responsibility to the commander.

activities.caption: true or false — the lessons beyond obedience
activities.name: socSurvivalJudge

statements.s: The prediction error is the finding — we systematically misjudge situational power.
statements.why: Because we do dispositions for others — the attribution errors at work.

statements.s: Milgram's deception and visible distress triggered modern ethics review, informed consent and debriefing norms.
statements.why: A science rebuilt, partly, on this experiment's controversy.

statements.s: Burger's 2009 partial replication, halted at 150 V, matched Milgram's compliance rate almost exactly.
statements.why: And cross-cultural versions from Munich to cross-national meta-analyses find the obedience gradient robust.

statements.s: The obedience finding failed to survive the modern replication era.
statements.why: It survived — the ethics norms changed, not the gradient.

activities.anchor: Asch then asked the sharper question
activities.caption: pair each conformity finding with its result
activities.name: socConformMatch

config.prompt: Conformity and its brakes — pair each study with its result:

pairs.right: norms being born: individual estimates converge into a group standard
about 75% conformed at least once to an obviously wrong majority — against a 1% solo error rate
conformity drops by around three-quarters — unanimity is load-bearing
conformity stronger in collectivist cultures — social machinery tuned by social values

config.why: Post-experiment interviews are the data's soul: some believed the majority, most knew better and went along anyway — normative pressure.

activities.caption: find the faulty line — a compliance briefing
activities.name: socComplySpot

config.prompt: One line of this compliance briefing is wrong — click it:
lines: The post-experiment interviews are the data's soul.
Most conformers knew better and went along anyway, under normative pressure.
A minority genuinely reported their perception distorting.
Belief change and public compliance have the same causes and the same brakes.
config.correction: They have different causes and different brakes — a private ballot or one dissenting ally collapses the compliance while leaving belief untouched.
config.why: Which is exactly why the split matters for practice.

activities.caption: file each attribution shortcut by name
activities.name: socAttribBuckets

config.prompt: File each attribution shortcut under its name:

items.label: readers who knew the writer was assigned a pro-Castro position still rated him as pro-Castro
I cut the lights because it's foggy; you cut them because you're reckless
my wins are skill, my losses are the referee
explaining others' behaviour by character and our own by circumstance

config.why: Kelley's covariation model — distinctiveness, consistency, consensus — is the ideal calculation the shortcuts bypass, and they explain why situational redesign beats lectures on character.

activities.anchor: hearing an apparent seizure over intercom
activities.caption: call the helping rate
activities.name: socBystanderEst

config.prompt: In Darley and Latané's intercom study, what share of participants who believed they were alone intervened during the apparent seizure?
config.why: About 85% alone — versus about 31% when others were believed present. Two mechanisms: responsibility divided among witnesses, and pluralistic ignorance — each witness reads the others' stillness as 'probably nothing'.
config.context: The Kitty Genovese tale of 38 indifferent neighbours became a lesson in media simplification — several people did call out or call police.

activities.anchor: a confederate staggers and collapses in a New York subway car
activities.caption: drag the divider — cane versus drunk
activities.name: socCaneCompare

config.prompt: The subway trial, two conditions — drag the divider.

before.label: the cane victim
before.text: Helped more often and faster — the perceived cost of helping, and of being wrong about danger, is lower.

after.label: the drunk victim
after.text: Helped less, and helpers were overwhelmingly same-race — a mild bias, weaker than expected.

config.why: Crucially, helping did not fall as the car filled: the victim collapsed at a specific passenger's feet, so responsibility was identifiable, not divided — the cost-reward calculus weighs helping costs against not-helping costs.

activities.caption: bet on what breaks the spell
activities.name: socFollowerPredict

config.q: Haslam and Reicher re-read Milgram's variations: which broke the spell of authority better?
config.why: Obedience as identification with a cause: participants who obeyed were engaged followers who believed in the science being served — which is why a dissenting second authority breaks the spell better than the victim's suffering does.
